Myriad also retains a 10% free-carried interest in Red Basin.

Three wholly owned projects. Different geological opportunities. Two countries.

Tomorrow’s uranium supply requires exploration investment today.

🇺🇸 A 92% headline premium puts U.S. #uranium M&A in focus.

Eagle #Nuclear Energy $NUCL has signed a binding LOI to acquire Noble Plains Uranium $NOBL in an all-share transaction.

The proposed terms:

▪️ 0.0167 Eagle shares per Noble Plains share
▪️ C$0.125 deemed value per share
▪️ ~92% premium to Noble Plains’ October 29 close

The strategic angle? Wyoming ISR potential alongside Eagle’s conventional uranium project in Oregon.
Duck Creek hosts 5.32M lbs indicated + 1.04M lbs inferred U₃O₈, reported on a 100% basis. Noble Plains holds an option to acquire 80%.
And that resource covers just 2.5 miles of a 5.25-mile trend, entirely within the shallower of two prospective formations. Room to explore.

My take: combining established resources, exploration upside and different development routes makes this worth watching.

Still an LOI: a definitive agreement and approvals remain outstanding. The all-share consideration also means the value moves with $NUCL.

The real test now: turning a larger U.S. uranium portfolio into future supply.

In May 1996, under the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, I used that inspiration to challenge private teams to fly a reusable spaceship to space twice within two weeks.

Behind me stood 20 astronauts, including Buzz Aldrin, plus Lindbergh’s grandson, Erik, and NASA Administrator Dan Goldin.

They thought I was being reckless, and in retrospect, I was.
The idea for creating this came from Lindbergh. In 1927, a $25,000 prize for the first nonstop flight from New York to Paris drove nine teams to spend $400,000. Only the winner got paid.

How I launched the first XPRIZE

Two board members resigned when I told them how much money I needed to launch the first XPRIZE. We had raised $500,000, and I wanted to spend it all announcing a $10 million competition. The truth was, I didn’t have the $10 million.

I call this launching “above the line of super-credibility.” When an idea is born above that line, people’s focus shifts from probabilities to implications. They stop asking whether it can happen and start asking HOW to be part of it.

Then I learned Anousheh Ansari wanted to fly on a suborbital flight. I pitched her, and she eventually said yes (after tracking her down while she was vacationing in Hawaii).

Here’s the truth, however: credibility didn’t make funding appear overnight. For five years, I pitched 150 people and heard the same questions every time: “Why isn’t NASA doing this? Can anyone really pull it off? Isn’t someone going to die trying?”

The reason I’m telling you all of this is that many of us have felt self-doubt or uncertainty about how to proceed when things get tough. Two board members calling you reckless is enough to make anyone doubt themselves. For five years, every “no” was a chance to quit.

Eventually, 26 teams invested more than $100 million chasing our $10 million prize. In 2004, SpaceShipOne won.

By then, all three questions had answers. NASA didn’t need to do it. A private team pulled it off. And no one was hurt.

The doubt will not go away on its own. You just need to stop letting it take control of your life.

So what’s the idea you’ve been waiting on, and what would it take to start before you feel ready?

Credibility got people to listen. Refusing to quit got it funded. Uncertain times don’t mean you should wait.

A lot of people are heading into hard years right now, unsure whether to bet on themselves. I understand that. I was there for five years with a $10 million promise and no $10 million.
